objectives.label: Got the restless bones to lie back down
Surprised the Seal-Keeper, which almost never happens

goal.text: Climb the mountain everyone else is running from, and give your answer.

steps.label: Climb up to the mountain's shoulder
Answer every question you are asked

facet_keystone.name: The Keystone
facet_keystone.text: The crown of the seal under Mount Red Sky. Bigger than your head, warm as a sleeping cat.

scene_tree_line.narration: The last tree on the mountain is a small, bent pine, and someone has nailed a sign to it: NO ROAD BEYOND THIS POINT. SERIOUSLY. Above it, Mount Red Sky goes up and up, glowing at the top like a lamp somebody forgot to turn off. Everyone else is running from this mountain. You are going to climb it, all the way to the seal deep inside, and give your answer. There are two ways on: an old stair that zigzags back and forth forever, or a slope of loose stones that goes straight up.

variants.text: Back at Redspire, Pellam wrote down what you are here for: to put the stones back, every one.
Back at Redspire, Pellam wrote down what you are here for: to finish the collection. Somewhere up there is the stone that would finish it.
Back at Redspire, Pellam wrote down what you are here for: to take the leash on what sleeps under the mountain, and hold it.

choices.label: Take the old zigzag stair
Scramble straight up the loose stones
Fly up ahead and pick the best way
Sing the Spiral Verses and let the path curl

scene_tree_line_stair.narration: The stair goes left, then right, then left, then right, about four hundred times. Somebody carved a tiny dragonling face on every hundredth step, and each face looks a little more tired than the last. By the top you are tired too, but it is a good tired, and the summit is a lot closer than it was.

choices.label: Keep climbing

check_scree.prompt: Scramble straight up the loose, sliding stones

onSuccess.narration: You go up like mountain goats, one quick foot after another, and the stones only slide where you just were. At the top you look down at the long zigzag stair everybody else would have taken, and feel extremely smug.

onFailure.narration: The slope slides, and you slide with it, sideways, like a sled, right onto the old stair halfway up. That was not the plan. It works anyway, and the dragonling face carved on the next step looks very surprised to see you.

scene_tree_line_fly.narration: You flap up over the mountain's shoulder, where the air is warm and smells of struck matches. From up here you can see the best way: a goat track nobody else noticed, hiding behind a big rock shaped like a sleeping cow. You land, point, and lead the way up it, trying very hard not to look pleased with yourself.

choices.label: Up the goat track

scene_tree_line_verses.narration: You sing the Spiral Verses in order, the way the relay taught them, and the path does a strange thing. It curls. Around a boulder, up a gully, past a ledge you would never have found, always gently uphill. Maybe the song was never really about the roads. Maybe it was about getting where the stones are going.

choices.label: Follow the curling path

scene_faun_family.narration: On the first slope, a faun family comes trotting downhill with everything they own on their backs, including a goat. The smallest one, Tansy, stops right in front of you and holds out a tiny pink stone. "It hums at night," she whispers. "It hummed louder when the ground shook. Is it my fault?" Her family waits for her, very politely, and very much wanting to keep running.

variants.text: You stop for breath and check your packs one more time. A few loose rush gems hum in the corners, the ordinary kind everybody carries, and that is all. Nothing anybody would climb a mountain to hand over. You came anyway. That is the whole point.
You stop for breath and check your packs one more time. Down among the rush gems: {facets} of the great stones. You know the story behind every one.

You stop for breath and check your packs one more time, and they clank. You are carrying {facets} great stones up a mountain. The mountain seems to know. A little shower of pebbles rattles down to meet you, like somebody clearing their throat.

choices.label: Promise to carry it up and put it back for her
Tell her it is only saying hello, and let her keep it
Show her the ford witch's sock trick

scene_faun_family_carry.narration: Tansy looks at the stone, and at the mountain, and at you. Then she puts it in your hand and folds your fingers over it, very seriously, like signing a contract. "Tell it sorry from me," she says. Then her family is off down the slope, the goat complaining the whole way. The little stone is warm. It is yours to carry now.

choices.label: Climb on, carrying it

scene_faun_family_hello.narration: "It is saying hello," you tell her. "Stones do that up here." Tansy holds it to her ear, and her face goes from worried to delighted. "Hello," she whispers back to it. Then she trots off downhill after her family, holding the stone to her ear the whole way, and the goat gives you a long look that says it is not convinced.

choices.label: Wave goodbye and climb on

scene_faun_family_sock.narration: You show her how the ford witch kept the Ford Stone: wrapped up snug in a thick wool sock, and kept warm. Tansy's mother pulls a sock out of a bundle at once. It is a very loud sock, striped orange and green. The pink stone goes in, and its hum goes soft as a purr. Tansy hugs the sock, and the family trots on downhill.

choices.label: Climb on

scene_wolf_ledge.narration: The path squeezes along a narrow ledge, and a whole pack of cinder wolves is lying across it. They are coming off the mountain like everybody else, and they have stopped to rest on the only warm rock. Nobody is growling. They look like dogs who have heard thunder and are pretending they have not. The biggest one opens one ember-colored eye.

choices.label: Tiptoe past along the cliff edge
Sit with them a minute, like with a worried dog
Give the big wolf a proper manticore nod
Let the Pride Stone hum, and see if they move

check_wolf_ledge.prompt: Tiptoe along the cliff edge past a pack of sleepy wolves

onSuccess.narration: You tiptoe so well that not one wolf wakes up. Well, one does, but only to roll over and stick all four paws in the air. You step over the paws, one at a time, holding your breath, and you are past.

onFailure.narration: A pebble clatters off the edge, and every wolf looks up at once. Then the big one sighs, gets up, and shuffles sideways to make room, like a grandpa on a crowded bench. You squeeze past, saying sorry to each wolf in turn.

scene_wolf_ledge_sit.narration: You sit down on the warm rock with them. After a while the big wolf leans on you, heavy and toasty as a stove. Every time the ground shakes, the whole pack shivers, and so do you, and then everybody feels a little better about it. When you finally get up to go, the wolves walk you to the end of the ledge, and no further.

choices.label: Climb on

scene_wolf_ledge_nod.narration: You give the big wolf the nod: chin down, tail still, one hunter to another, very proper. The big wolf looks at you for a long moment. Then it nods back, gets up, and leads the whole pack off the ledge in single file so you can pass. The smallest wolf stares at your tail the whole way. Professional courtesy is old, and it still works.

choices.label: Climb on

scene_wolf_ledge_pride.narration: You let the Pride Stone hum in your pack. The wolves' ears go flat. One by one they get up and slink off the ledge into the rocks, the same way the prides would never den near it. The way is clear. It is also very quiet, and the warm rock is empty, and you are not sure you like being the thing that wolves get out of the way of.

choices.label: Climb on, a bit quieter

scene_warden_post.narration: Higher up, the wardens' last post sits on a ledge with nobody in it. On the table is a big logbook, open to today, with a pencil on a string and a sign in very neat letters: ALL CLIMBERS MUST SIGN IN. Under it, a smaller sign: THIS MEANS YOU. Nobody has signed in all day. Beside the log is a little box labeled FOR CLIMBERS WHO SIGNED.

variants.text: You told the wardens everything, back at Redspire, and somebody here was expecting you. At the top of today's page, in very neat writing, it already says: THE ONES WHO TOLD US. PLEASE SIGN BELOW.
Somebody has tied a tiny bell to the pencil string, the grandmothers' kind. The news you took to the dragonling towns got up the mountain before you did.
Nobody up here knows you are coming. You kept it close, and the empty post keeps your secret too.

choices.label: Sign in properly, in your very best writing
Sign in as Sir Pancake and the Cookie Twins
Find tag 4117 in the log, and write FOUND
Leave the wardens a note: we went up

scene_warden_post_sign.narration: You sign in properly, every name at the table, in your very best writing. Under WHERE TO you write: the bottom. Under BACK BY you write nothing, because nobody knows. The little box clicks open. Inside is a warden's mosslight jar, glowing green, with a label: FOR THE WAY DOWN. Somebody thought about you getting back. That helps more than you expected.

choices.label: Climb on

scene_warden_post_silly.narration: You sign in as Sir Pancake and the Cookie Twins, and under REASON FOR CLIMB you write: snacks. You laugh so hard that the next steep bit of path goes by without anyone noticing it was steep. The little box stays shut. It is a warden box. It knows. Somewhere in the future, a warden is going to write a very confused report about three cookies.

choices.label: Climb on, still laughing

scene_warden_post_clerks.narration: You flip back through the log until you find it: TAG 4117. STATUS: MISSING. Underlined three times. Somebody has been very upset about tag 4117. You take the pencil on its string and, next to MISSING, you write: FOUND, AND GOING HOME. The little box clicks open for that, too. Inside is a mosslight jar, glowing green, labeled FOR THE WAY DOWN.

choices.label: Climb on

scene_warden_post_note.narration: You tear a page from the back of the log and write: To the wardens. We went up. You know what for. You fold it into a warden-neat square and set it on top of the log, exactly straight, where a warden will look first. It feels like keeping a promise to people who keep all of theirs. The little box clicks open. Inside is a mosslight jar, glowing green.

choices.label: Climb on

scene_overlook.narration: At the mountain's shoulder the clouds pull apart, and suddenly you can see the whole realm at once: the city where you started, the green fields, the river roads and the rush roads and the dark forest roads, all of them winding north to right here. Tiny lights crawl along every one of them, going the other way. Somewhere down there is everything that happened to you.

choices.label: Find home, all the way south
Don't look back. Look up.
Find the Great River, all the way down
Find the caravan road, and hum the relay-song
Find the forest, and MossHome inside it

scene_overlook_home.narration: You find it: a tiny smudge, very far south, about the size of your thumbnail. Somebody there is probably having dinner. You stand and look at the thumbnail for a while, and nobody says anything, and that turns out to be exactly the right thing to say. Then you turn around. Home will still be there. That is the whole point of going up.

choices.label: Turn around and climb

scene_overlook_up.narration: You turn your back on all of it and look up instead. The summit is close now, glowing red at the edges like a coal somebody just blew on. "Nobody look back," somebody says. Then everybody looks back, just once, very quickly. Then up again. Everybody agrees that it still counts as not looking back, if you are quick.

variants.text: You turn your back on all of it and look up instead. The summit is close now, glowing red at the edges like a coal somebody just blew on. "Don't look back," you tell yourself, out loud, because there is nobody else to tell. Then you look back, just once, very quickly. Then up again. You decide that still counts as not looking back, if you are quick.

choices.label: Climb

scene_overlook_river.narration: You find the Great River, a silver ribbon running all the way down the realm, and on it a tiny dot that might be a flat boat with a frog in a very old hat. It is much too far to be sure. But the dot stops moving, the way a boat would stop if somebody on it had just looked up a mountain. Then it drifts on downstream.

choices.label: Climb on

scene_overlook_rush.narration: You find the caravan road, the busiest road in the realm, and you hum the relay-song down at it. It is a very long way down. But a moment later, faint as a whisper, the next line comes floating back up on the wind, sung by a hundred travelers all going the other way. The relay never stops. Not even now. Not even for this.

choices.label: Climb on, humming

scene_overlook_wild.narration: You find the forest, a dark green blanket over half the realm, and somewhere in the middle of it, MossHome. As you look, the whole forest sways at once, every tree together, like a crowd waving. It is probably the wind. It is probably not the wind. You wave back, just in case, and a little way down the slope a raven pretends not to have seen.

choices.label: Climb on

choice_cairn.narration: Near the top of the path stands a cairn: a tall pile of stones, each one left by somebody who climbed this far. Some have names scratched on them. Some have little drawings. One is wearing a tiny knitted hat. You leave something on the cairn before the last climb. That is the rule, and nobody remembers who made it. Everybody vote: what do we leave?

choices.label: A pebble with every name in the party on it
A pebble with a secret wish whispered into it
Our last snack, for whoever climbs up next
Our names, carved as BIG as they will go
Read the very oldest stone first

choice_cairn_names.narration: You scratch all your names onto a pebble and set it carefully near the top. It looks very small up there, among all the other names. But it is there now, and it will still be there tomorrow, and the day after that, whatever happens down below. That is what a cairn is for. The whole pile creaks a little, as if making room.

variants.text: You scratch your name onto a pebble and set it carefully near the top. One pebble, one name. It looks very small up there, among all the other names. But it is there now, and it will still be there tomorrow, and the day after that, whatever happens down below. That is what a cairn is for. The whole pile creaks a little, as if making room for exactly one more.

choices.label: Climb on

choice_cairn_wish.narration: You whisper a wish into the same pebble, taking turns, and nobody tells anybody what they wished. You set it on the cairn. For a moment the pebble feels warm, though that might just be your hands. You walk on, all of you pretending you are not trying to guess each other's wishes. Everybody is trying to guess.

variants.text: You whisper a wish into a pebble, so quietly that the mountain has to lean in to hear it. You set it on the cairn. For a moment the pebble feels warm, though that might just be your hands. You walk on and keep the wish to yourself. That is what secret wishes are for.

choices.label: Climb on

choice_cairn_snack.narration: You set your very last snack on the cairn, wrapped up neatly, for whoever climbs up next. It is like the empty chair every table at the Exchange keeps for whoever arrives. Your stomachs grumble about it all the way up. But someday somebody tired is going to find a snack on top of a mountain, and that is a very good feeling to carry.

choices.label: Climb on, hungry and pleased

choice_cairn_big_names.narration: You carve your names as big as they will go. They go very big. Then you run out of stone, and the last name has to go around the back and up the side, and one letter ends up on a different stone altogether. Climbers for years will read it and wonder who on earth MAGNIFICEN was. It is still, honestly, very impressive.

choices.label: Climb on, magnificently

choice_cairn_oldest.narration: The oldest stone is right at the bottom, its name worn almost smooth. You trace it with a finger. It is not a name you know. But under it someone scratched a tiny drawing: a dragon, a round window, and a little stick figure waving. Somebody climbed up here a very, very long time ago, for the same reason you did. You set your pebble right beside it.

choices.label: Climb on

scene_bell_hut.narration: Just below the summit is the highest bell-hut in the foothills, where the dragonlings start the bell-code on its way down. It is empty. The bell rope is tied tight to a hook, with a note: GONE DOWN. TIED SO NOBODY RINGS THE LAST ONE BY ACCIDENT. There is just enough slack for an ordinary ring. Far below, every bell is quiet, holding its breath.

variants.text: Your packs are so light on this last steep bit that you could almost run. The wind up here keeps tugging at them, as if it is checking for something. There is nothing inside but rush gems and crumbs, and the wind goes away looking puzzled.
Up here, your packs hum louder than ever. Inside, carried all this way: {facets} of the great stones. You could tell the story of every one.

Up here, every step is heavier, and the path knows why. You have carried {facets} great stones nearly to the top. Little stones skitter away from your boots as you pass, and the bell rope sways, though there is no wind.

choices.label: Ring the all's well, for everyone below
Leave it be, and tie a second knot to be sure
Ring it properly, the way your family does

check_bell_code.prompt: Remember the bell-code for all's well

onSuccess.narration: Two long, one short, two long. You get it exactly right. The ring rolls down the mountain, and the next hut rings it back, and the next, and the next, all the way into the foothills: all's well, all's well. It is not quite true yet. It is a promise, and now everybody has heard you make it.

onFailure.narration: Two long, one short? Or one short, two long? You ring it anyway. Far below, the next hut pauses, as if it is checking. Then it rings it back, and the next hut does too, and the next. It is not all's well. It is something else entirely.

scene_soup_ring.narration: It is the soup's ready ring. All the way down the mountain, every bell-hut in the foothills is now ringing soup's ready, one after another, very cheerfully. Somewhere down there, thousands of frightened people stop running for a moment and think about soup. That is not nothing. Honestly, it might be better than all's well.

choices.label: Climb on, still giggling

scene_bell_hut_knot.narration: You tie a second knot, a good one, and then a third, because three is a nice number. Nobody is ringing anything by accident while you are around. As you leave, the old hut creaks in the wind, as if it had been worrying about that rope all day and can finally stop. You feel a bit like a bell-keeper yourself.

choices.label: Climb on

scene_bell_hut_family.narration: You ring it the family way: two long, one short, two long, with the little flick at the end that only grandmothers bother with. The ring rolls down the mountain, and the huts below answer one by one: all's well. Then one very far hut adds a flick at the end, just like yours. Somebody down there knows exactly who is ringing.

choices.label: Climb on

scene_crab_field.narration: The path crosses a field of gray ash, and the field is covered in gems. Big ones, glittering, just lying there. Except every so often, a gem blinks. They are glassback crabs, hundreds of them, pretending to be a gem deposit so nobody will dig them up. It is not a very good plan. Several of them are already waving their claws at you, in a way that clearly means something.

choices.label: Read their claw-waving, and walk where they say
Go the long way around the field
Out-pretend them with an even better act
Let them hear your collection, and see what happens

check_crab_field.prompt: Read what the glassback crabs are waving about

onSuccess.narration: Claw up means not here. Claw sideways means fine, go on. You read them like a signpost and walk a wiggly line right across the field, and not one crab gets stepped on. At the far side, one waves both claws at once. You decide that means well done.

onFailure.narration: You read go on where it clearly said absolutely not, and step right onto a crab. It is not hurt, only very offended, and it holds onto your bootlace all the way across like a ticket. At the far side it lets go and clatters back to its spot, muttering in crab.

scene_crab_field_around.narration: You take the long way around, along the edge of the ash, where nobody is pretending to be anything. It takes ages. Halfway around, the whole field of crabs shuffles slowly sideways to keep an eye on you, glittering, like the world's most suspicious audience. When you reach the far side, they all settle down and go back to being gems.

choices.label: Climb on

scene_crab_field_glitter.narration: You crouch down, go perfectly still, and glitter. Somehow, you glitter. The crabs stare. One by one they decide you are a much better gem deposit than they are, and they shuffle aside in deep professional jealousy. You cross the whole field one sparkly step at a time. Nobody will ever believe this. You are going to tell it anyway.

choices.label: Climb on, sparkling

scene_crab_field_collection.narration: You open your pack a crack, and the collection hums. Every crab in the field stops pretending. Hundreds of tiny eyes turn to stare at your pack, as if they have just met the biggest gem deposit in the world, and it is walking. They part to let you through without a single wave. You are not sure that was respect. It felt a little like being a mountain.

variants.text: You open your pack a crack, and your few rush gems hum. The crabs stop pretending, just for a moment, and stare. Then they look at each other, and you can almost hear them thinking: is that it? They part to let you through anyway, the way you make room for somebody small. It is not respect, exactly. It is a little bit like kindness.
Behind you, the whole ash field sinks a finger's width, as if {facets} great stones walking across it were more than it could quite hold.

choices.label: Climb on

scene_ember_drift.narration: Near the top, something tiny glows in a drift of gray ash: one embermoth, stuck up to its wings, blinking slowly like a nightlight running low. Every moth out here on the slopes has flown away from the mountain, all except the old ones deep inside it, which never leave. This one must have turned around too late, or too early. It looks up at you the way a lost puppy looks at the first nice person it sees.

choices.label: Dig it out, carefully, with your hands
Scoop it up, ash and all, and carry it with you
Hold the Ember Facet close, so it can find the warm
Use the tiny woven broom someone left by the drift

check_ember_drift.prompt: Dig the embermoth out of the ash without squashing it

onSuccess.narration: You dig very gently, like digging out a sandcastle you want to keep. The moth pops free, shakes the ash off its wings, and zooms ahead of you up the path, glowing brighter every second, as if it is showing you the way.

onFailure.narration: You dig too fast, and ash flies everywhere, mostly up your nose. While you are busy sneezing, the moth wriggles out all by itself, gives you a very dignified look, and flies off uphill ahead of you. It definitely did that on purpose.

scene_ember_drift_carry.narration: You scoop it up, ash and all, and cup it in your hands. The moth is warm, like holding the last bit of a campfire. It sits there blinking at you, and slowly it glows a little brighter. Nobody can climb with both hands full, so your pack rides high on your back, and the moth rides in your cupped hands, very carefully, the rest of the way up.

choices.label: Climb on, carrying it

scene_ember_drift_ember.narration: You hold the Ember Facet close to the drift, your very first stone. The moth crawls out of the ash and straight onto it, as if it had been looking for exactly this all along. It curls up on the warm stone like a cat on a hearth and goes to sleep. So now you are carrying it up the mountain too. You do not mind one bit.

choices.label: Climb on, carrying it

scene_ember_drift_broom.narration: Leaning on a rock by the drift is a broom no bigger than your finger, woven out of straw, with a tiny medal on it that says HELP. Nobody is around. Nobody ever is, when the sprites are being kind. You sweep the moth free in three neat strokes, and it flies off uphill ahead of you, glowing. When you look back, the broom is gone.

choices.label: Climb on

choice_last_breath.narration: At the very top, the path ends at a dark round hole in the mountain: a lava tube, breathing warm air out at you, slow and steady, like something asleep. The stones in your packs are humming so loudly now you can feel it in your teeth. This is it. Before you go in, everybody vote: what do we do with our last minute outside?

choices.label: Tell each other the best bit of the whole road
Count the great stones, one more time
Count what you did bring
Practice what you will say when you give them back
Polish the collection until it shines in the dark
Check the tether one last time

choice_last_breath_best.narration: You each tell the best bit. Nobody picks the same one. One of you picks something so small the others had forgotten it, and then everybody remembers, and laughs. It turns out most of the best bits were the soggy bits. The tube breathes out warm air, patiently, as if it has been listening and does not mind waiting one more minute.

variants.text: You tell the best bit out loud, to the mountain, since it is the only one here to listen. Then you think of another best bit, and another, and you laugh at one so small you had almost forgotten it. It turns out most of the best bits were the soggy bits. The tube breathes out warm air, patiently, as if it has been listening and does not mind waiting one more minute.

choices.label: Go in

choice_last_breath_count.narration: You tip the stones out on a flat rock and count them, one more time. They hum together, each a little different, like a choir warming up. You remember where every single one came from, and who was there, and what it cost. Then you pack them away again, carefully, the way you pack something that was never exactly yours.

variants.text: You tip out your one great stone on a flat rock and look at it, one more time. It hums by itself, a small steady note. It is the one you would have picked anyway. You remember the day you found it, and who was there, and what it cost. Then you pack it away again, carefully, the way you pack something that was never exactly yours.

You tip out the great stones on a flat rock and count them, one more time: {facets}. They hum together, each a little different, like a very small choir warming up. You remember where every one came from, and who was there, and what it cost. Then you pack them away again, carefully, the way you pack something that was never exactly yours.

You tip out the great stones on a flat rock and count them out loud. It takes a while, because there are {facets} great stones, and the rock creaks under them. They hum together like a whole choir warming up, and far below, the mountain hums back, as if it has been counting along. You remember where every one came from. Then you pack them away again, and the packs are very heavy, the way something is heavy when it was never exactly yours.

choices.label: Go in

choice_last_breath_count_brought.narration: You turn out your pockets on a flat rock and count what is there. A few rush gems, humming like everybody's. Some crumbs. A bit of string. A keepsake or two from the road that nobody else would look at twice. Then you count the things that do not fit in pockets: the people who waved you on, the promises you made, the friends who helped you along the way and the ones waiting at home. That count is much longer. It takes the whole minute, and it is worth more than a mountain of stones.

choices.label: Go in

choice_last_breath_practice.narration: You practice what you will say when you give the stones back. "Here you are." Too short. "We are very sorry about the whole entire rush." Too long. "These are yours." That one is right. You say it out loud, three times, until it sounds like you mean it. You do mean it. That was never the hard part.

choices.label: Go in

choice_last_breath_polish.narration: You polish every stone in the collection on your sleeves until they shine, even in the shadow of the tube. Laid out on the rock, they glow in a rough circle, with one space left at the top. Nobody says anything about the space. Everybody looks at it. Then you pack them up and go in to find what fills it.

variants.text: You polish what you have on your sleeves: a few rush gems, the ordinary humming kind. Laid out on the rock, they make a very small circle with a great deal of space in it. Nobody says anything about the space. Everybody looks at it. Then you pack them up and go in, to see what a collection with nothing in it can still do.

choices.label: Go in

choice_last_breath_tether.narration: You check the tether one last time: what you borrowed, what you promised, what you made up on the way. It is all there, or most of it is. You tie a knot in the last bit of string you have, for luck. It is not a leash. It might be the start of one. It is going to have to do.

choices.label: Go in

scene_mouth.narration: You step into the lava tube, a tunnel the mountain made for itself long ago. It opens into a gallery where the walls glitter with gem-veins, like fireworks frozen halfway through going off. Then the old bones set into the rock begin, very slowly, to stand up. They are not looking at you. They are looking at your pockets.

variants.text: There is not much in your pockets but rush gems and crumbs. The bones look anyway, puzzled, the way a dog sniffs an empty hand.
Along the walls, the gem-veins light up one after another as you pass, following your packs. You carry {facets} great stones, and the whole gallery has noticed.

choices.label: Help the bones lie back down, gently
Stand your ground
Set the Table Stone back into the vein
Set the Ember Facet back into the wall

You kept it close the whole way, and you keep it close now. Some nights, far up the mountain, a tiny bell rings the happy ring all by itself, and you know the mountain remembers.

ending_collectors.narration: You lift the crown stone, the one the wardens' oldest logs call the Keystone. It is warm, and it is yours, and whatever you were collecting, it is complete now. The seal holds, just, the way a door holds without a lock, because the Seal-Keeper lies down across it and stays there, and means to stay. The rush is over and you won it. History files you as The Collectors, and the red sky is no longer the strangest weather in the realm. You are. Somewhere a grandmother adds your names to a very old list, and leaves a space under them, in case.

variants.text: History notes one odd thing about The Collectors: they climbed the mountain with empty hands. The Keystone was the first stone they ever kept, and the last.
Your collection is small and very heavy at the top: {facets} great stones, and one of them is bigger than your head.
With the Keystone, your collection is {facets} great stones. The packs are so heavy that the mountain groans when you lift them, and every crab on the ash field turns to watch you carry them down.
You came north for the treasure, and you got the biggest one there is. It is very heavy, and it hums all the way home.
You came to find out what really happened. The answer is in your hands, the size of your head, and it will not stop humming.
You came so everyone would know your names. Everyone does. Some say them with a cheer, and some with a frown.
You came because somebody had to keep folk safe. The Seal-Keeper is keeping them safe now, lying across the crack. You visit it every spring, with snacks.
You came for a fresh start. With a stone like this, you could start anything at all. You are still deciding what.
You came to prove you could do it. Nobody had ever lifted the Keystone before. Now somebody has.
Hessa comes to see the Keystone once. She looks at it for a long time and says nothing, and leaves you a pot of soup anyway.
Hessa's masked singers from the soup tent ask, very politely, if they may sing to the Keystone. You let them, once a year, and the stone hums back.
The wardens log the Keystone twice, then a third time, then post a warden outside your door, very politely, forever. The warden turns out to be excellent at checkers.
The grandmothers make up a brand-new ring for you. Nobody is sure yet whether it means thank you or watch out. The little ones ring it anyway, because it is fun.

You told nobody you were going, and now you hold the one stone everybody wants. You keep it close, the way you kept everything else. It hums, very softly, like a cat that has decided you are its people.

ending_wardens_regret.narration: Down the last tube come the Skywardens, a whole citadel of them, out of breath and still very neat about it. You put the leash into the hands of their captain, a very tidy warden called Captain Voss. They build a cage of oaths and ledgers around the titan, and it holds: honest, careful and cold. The realm is safe the way a locked room is safe. Years later, the wardens' captain writes one line in a ledger of a different color: I wonder if it was lonely. History calls it The Wardens' Regret. And the embermoths still visit the titan every evening, because nobody ever told them not to.

variants.text: In the wardens' ledger, beside your names, the column for STONES SURRENDERED says: none. The captain leaves it like that. She thinks it is the most honest line in the book.
In the wardens' ledger, beside your names, the column for STONES SURRENDERED says {facets}, written very neatly, and checked twice.

In the wardens' ledger, the column for STONES SURRENDERED runs off the bottom of the page: {facets} great stones, each one logged twice. It is the longest entry the citadel has ever written, and the wardens are very proud of it.
You came north for the treasure. The wardens give you a receipt for the leash instead. It is the most carefully written thing you will ever own.
You came to find out what really happened. The wardens let you read every log about it, all four hundred years, which takes most of a winter.
You came so everyone would know your names. The wardens write them on the cage, very small, in the corner, logged twice.
You came because somebody had to keep folk safe. The wardens agree with you completely, which turns out to be more worrying than you expected.
You came for a fresh start. The wardens offer you a job. You say you will think about it, and you mean it.
You came to prove you could do it. Captain Voss shakes your hand, which she has never done for anyone. Nobody at the citadel ever forgets it.
Hessa hears about the cage. She does not argue. She sends the titan a song every evening, along with the moths.
Hessa writes you a letter about the coins you gave her soup tents: she would like them spent on something kinder than a cage. You keep the letter.
You told the wardens first, and they never forget it. Pellam keeps a chair for you at the truth-table, with a cushion on it, which is not regulation.
The grandmothers ring a slow ring every evening for whatever is in the cage. The wardens tried to stop them once. They have stopped trying, and some of them hum along.
You kept it close all the way to the bottom, and then you gave it away. The wardens are still not sure what to make of you, which is the closest wardens come to liking someone.

ending_cure.narration: Hessa's people, the Deep Hollow choir, sing their crystal chord into the seal, and you hold them to every word. Something under the mountain hums back. Hessa's choir swears the world's broken laws are mending, and maybe they are: the sky is a little less red, and Hessa cries into a pot of soup. History calls it The Cure, with a question mark that nobody has ever quite been able to rub out.

variants.text: The choir writes a song about you afterwards: the climbers who carried nothing up the mountain. It is a short song. Hessa says the short ones are the truest.
Your great stones sing in the chord too, a few small notes of their own, {facets} in all.
The choir sets your {facets} great stones around the seal in a ring, and the chord gets so loud that windows rattle in the foothills. Hessa says she has never heard a chord like it. She cries again.
You came north for the treasure. Hessa pays you in soup, every day, for the rest of your life, and honestly it is a fair price.
You came to find out what really happened. Hessa says you will have to wait and see, like everybody else. You find you do not mind.
You came so everyone would know your names. The choir sings them in a chord, which is the loudest way a name can be said.
You came because somebody had to keep folk safe. Whether this keeps them safe, nobody knows yet, so you keep watching, just in case.
You came for a fresh start. Hessa says the whole world is having one now. She may even be right.
You came to prove you could do it. You held a whole choir to its word, which most people will tell you cannot be done.
You said no to Hessa's cure once, at a soup tent in the foothills. Then you handed it to her anyway. She laughs about that for years.
The coins you gave the soup tents helped pay for the choir's crystal chord. Hessa shows you the receipt, very proudly.
The wardens write it all down twice, add a question mark, and send a warden to sing with the choir and keep an eye on things. The warden turns out to have a lovely voice.
The grandmothers ring a new ring for the choir, and the choir sings one back. By spring, nobody can tell which is which.
You kept it close until the very end, and then you trusted Hessa with it. She keeps that trust like her best ladle, polished and always close at hand.

ending_new_weather.narration: You hold the leash, and the power under the mountain lies still in your own hands. The realm gains something new: you. Farmers watch your camp to know if it will rain. Wolf packs set their routes by your fires. History is not sure what to call you, so it calls you The New Weather, and the Seal-Keeper sometimes visits for tea.

variants.text: People say you came up the mountain with nothing in your packs. It is true, and somehow it is why the farmers trust you.
You keep what you carried, {facets} of the great stones, in a jar by the fire. On stormy nights the jar hums, and the farmers take that to mean: bring in the washing.

You keep all {facets} great stones in a row along your windowsill. When they hum together, the whole valley gets a thunderstorm, so people learn to listen for it. The mountain still shivers when you visit.
You came north for the treasure. Now farmers bring you pies to ask about the weather, which is better than treasure, mostly.
You came to find out what really happened. Now you find out every morning, because you are what happens.
You came so everyone would know your names. Every farmer in the realm says them each morning, looking up at the sky.
You came because somebody had to keep folk safe. Now you keep the weather kind, too.
You came for a fresh start. You got the freshest one there is: being something the realm never had before.
You came to prove you could do it. You hold the power under a mountain in your hands. Nobody asks you to prove anything anymore.
Hessa comes for tea sometimes, on the same days as the Seal-Keeper. They argue very politely about the cure, and you pour.
Hessa writes to thank you for the coins you gave her soup tents, and asks, very politely, for rain on Tuesdays.
The wardens send a clerk to log the weather at your camp twice a day. Pellam asks for the job, and gets it.
The grandmothers make up a ring for every kind of weather you make. The rain ring is the little ones' favorite.
You kept it close the whole way, and you are keeping it close still: the power under the mountain, folded in your hands like a sleeping bird.

ending_turned_back.narration: The Seal-Keeper does not hurt children who came up the mountain the wrong way. It removes them, and sets you down in the foothills next to everybody else. Then it goes back down to hold the seal alone, for as long as it can. You watch the summit glow all night with the rest of the realm. At dawn an embermoth lands on your hand and stays, which it only does for someone it expects to see again.

variants.text: You came down with nothing, the same as you went up. Somehow that makes the embermoth's choice even clearer.
Your packs still hold {facets} of the great stones. They hum all night, very softly, toward the mountain.

The Seal-Keeper set you down with all {facets} great stones still in your packs. They hum all night toward the summit, so loudly that nobody nearby gets any sleep, and so the whole foothills keeps watch with you.
You came north for the treasure. Tonight you would trade every gem in the realm to be back up there, helping.
You came to find out what really happened. You will find out, one way or another. You are not done asking.
You came so everyone would know your names. Tonight nobody says them. Tomorrow, maybe, somebody will.
You came because somebody had to keep folk safe. Somebody still has to. You will be ready next time.
You came for a fresh start. This is not the one you wanted, but it is still a start.
You came to prove you could do it. You have not proved it yet. Yet is a very important word.
Hessa brings soup to the foothills for everyone keeping watch. She gives you the first bowl, and the biggest.
Hessa's masked singers from the soup tent sing to the mountain all night. You are not sure it helps. You sing along anyway.
In Redspire, Pellam opens a fresh page and writes your names at the top, with a space beneath them. "For next time," he says.
The grandmothers ring the ordinary bell all night, so the Keeper knows it is not holding alone. You ring it with them.
Nobody knew you went up. Nobody knows you came down. But you know, and the embermoth knows, and that is enough to start again.

ending_last_ring.narration: The ring nobody had ever used rings out across the whole realm. The mountain shrugs, and something enormous stretches underneath it, and there is nobody at the seal to answer. The realm does not end. It rearranges: rivers wander, roads bend, the red sky becomes ordinary weather. History files you as the almost-heroes. But down in the foothills, a dragonling child is already learning the bell code backwards, in case there is a ring that puts it all to sleep again.

variants.text: History adds that you carried no stones at all. Some people think that makes it sadder. The dragonling child thinks it makes it braver.
In your packs, the last bell sets off a faint ring from {facets} of the great stones, and then everything goes quiet.
In your packs, all {facets} great stones ring along with the last bell, loud as a second bell, and every mountain in the realm hears it.
You came north for the treasure. Now the treasure is scattered across a brand-new map, and you start learning where it all fell.
You came to find out what really happened. Now there is a whole new realm to find out about.
You came so everyone would know your names. They know you as the almost-heroes. You plan to drop the almost.
You came because somebody had to keep folk safe. Folk are scattered, not gone, and you go to find them, one town at a time.
You came for a fresh start. The whole realm gets one now, whether it wanted one or not, and somebody has to help.
You came to prove you could do it. You nearly did. Nearly is how the second half of every great story starts.
Hessa's soup tents are the first thing open in the new realm. She does not talk about the cure anymore. She just ladles.
The coins you gave the soup tents buy blankets for everyone whose roof wandered off. Hessa makes sure of it.
The wardens start a brand-new log on the very first morning: WHERE EVERYTHING WENT. You help them fill it in.
The grandmothers ring every bell they have left, to find each other in the new realm. One by one, far away, the bells answer.
Nobody knew you went up. But you know where the seal is now, and you have not stopped thinking about how to fix it.

ending_broken_tether.narration: The leash snaps. The seal cracks instead of holding, and the titan rolls over, half awake, and the mountain throws gemstones across the whole sky. The Seal-Keeper throws itself across the crack and holds it, and keeps on holding. Everybody who reached for that leash grieves, which is the worst part. But the seal is cracked, not broken, and the Keeper is still holding. Holding is something somebody can help with, someday.

variants.text: Later, the Keeper says you had nothing to hold it with but your hands, and you held it anyway. That counts, it says. It counts for a lot.
Afterward, your packs still hum with {facets} of the great stones, pulling toward the crack as if they want to help hold it. Someday they might.
Afterward, your packs still hold all {facets} great stones, every one pulling toward the crack. They are exactly what a cracked seal needs. Someday somebody will carry them down to it.
You came north for the treasure. Now the sky is full of it, and you spend the next year helping people pick it up.
You came to find out what really happened. Now you know more about the titan than anybody alive, and someday that will help.
You came so everyone would know your names. The Keeper knows them, and calls them when it needs a hand. That is a good kind of famous.
You came because somebody had to keep folk safe. The Keeper is keeping them safe now, and you go back every week to help it hold.
You came for a fresh start. The realm has a crack in it now, and fresh starts are how cracks get mended.
You came to prove you could do it. You could not, this time. You are already working out how you will.
You said no to Hessa's cure once. Now she is the first to climb down and help hold the crack, and you hold it side by side.
Hessa's masked singers from the soup tent grieve loudest of anyone. Then they start singing again, very softly, to help the Keeper hold.
The wardens come up with ropes and ledgers, and start writing down exactly how to hold a cracked seal. You help with the ropes.
The grandmothers send a bell-keeper to sit with the Keeper every night, so it is never holding alone.
You kept it close, and now it is yours to help mend. You go back up the mountain in the spring, with better hands.

check_tether_self_bare.prompt: Hold the leash with nothing but your own hands

onSuccess.narration: No tether this time, only hands, so you become the tether. It pulls, and pulls, and then settles in your hands. The Seal-Keeper blinks, which it has not done in a very long time.

onFailure.narration: Bare hands are not enough. It pulls once, hard, and slips through every hand on it.

check_tether_cult_bare.narration: You call up the tube for Hessa, and she comes at once, as if she had been waiting on the stair all along. Behind her come her friends from the Deep Hollow in their painted bark masks, humming one low note. Hessa looks at the leash, then at your empty hands. "We'll sing," she says. "Tell us the bargain, and we'll keep it."
check_tether_cult_bare.prompt: Hold Hessa's singers to a bargain you made up just now

onSuccess.narration: You make the bargain up as you go, and you make it very carefully. Hessa reads it twice and nods. They keep every word.

onFailure.narration: Nobody wrote the bargain down, so Hessa's singers sing it the way they remember it. One note more than you meant. It is enough, and Hessa's face falls before anyone else's.

scene_keystone.narration: The crown stone is bigger than your head and warm as bread. The Seal-Keeper does not stop you. It only watches, and says: "Everyone who climbs reaches for it once. Most of them have no idea what they would do with it."

variants.text: Your hands are all you brought to hold it with. They look very small next to it.
Behind you, {facets} great stones hum in your packs, louder and louder, as if they know exactly what is about to join them.

check_keystone.prompt: Pry the crown stone out of a seal that does not want to let it go

onSuccess.narration: It comes loose with a sound like a cork from the biggest bottle in the world. You did not come up here for this. You are holding it anyway.

onFailure.narration: The crown stone does not budge. Then the Seal-Keeper puts one claw on it, very gently, and the decision is no longer yours.
